Access to Hydroxy-Functionalized Polypropylene through
Coordination Polymerization
Yuanhao Zhong, Iskander Douair, Tiantian Wang, Chunji Wu,* Laurent Maron,* and
Dongmei Cui*
Abstract: Preparation of polyethylenes containing hydroxy
groups has been already industrialized through radical copoly-
merization under harsh conditions followed by alcoholysis. By
contrast, hydroxy-functionalized polypropylene has proven
a rather challenging goal in polymer science. Propylene can/C29t
be polymerized through a radical mechanism, and its coordi-
nation copolymerization with polar monomers is frustrated by
catalyst poisoning. Herein, we report a new strategy to reach
this target. The coordination polymerization of allenes by rare-
earth-metal precursors affords pure 1,2-regulated polyallenes,
which are facilely transformed into poly(allyl alcohol) ana-
logues by subsequent hydroboration/oxidation. Strikingly, the
copolymerization of allenes and propylene gives unprece-
dented hydroxy-functionalized polypropylene after post-poly-
merization modification. Mechanistic elucidation by DFT
simulation suggests kinetic rather than thermodynamic control.
The synthesis of hydroxy-functionalized (co)polymers, in
particular polyolefins, has been a major focus of polymer
scientists because the hydroxy group endows the materials
with hydrophilicity and excellent surface properties, and
furthermore, it is a reactive group that enables access to other
functionalities. For instance, polyethylene (PE) is the most
famous and widely applied hydrophobic plastic,
[1] whilst its
hydroxy-functionalized derivatives such as poly(vinyl alco-
hol) (PV A) and poly(ethylene-vinyl alcohol) (EVOH) pos-
sess rather unique properties and applications in different
fields.
[2] To date the copolymerization of ethylene with
a broad scope of functional vinyl monomers has been
thoroughly investigated and achieved great successes,
[3]
except for hydroxy functionalization. Fortunately, radical
polymerization of vinyl acetate or copolymerization with
ethylene under high temperature and pressure followed by
post-polymerization alcoholysis affords PV A and EVOH,
which is a rather efficient industrialized method.
[4] By
contrast, synthesis of the corresponding hydroxy-functional-
ized polypropylene (PP) from the direct polymerization of
allylic alcohol (AA) or its copolymerization with propylene
poses serious problems. Although allyl alcohol (AA) is
a stable chemical, it is hard to propagate into a high molecular
weight P AA through radical polymerization even with the
assistance of a Lewis acid;
[5] furthermore anionic and
coordination catalysts react with the hydroxy group rather
than the C =C bond. A more efficient manner of obtaining
a linear P AA with high molecular weight (ca. 30 kDa) and
a block copolymer with styrene P(AA-St) was reported
recently by Hillmyer and co-workers through reversible
addition–fragmentation chain transfer (RAFT) radical poly-
merization of the Boc-protected (bis(tert-butyloxy carbon-
ate)) vinyl ester or vinyl amide followed by post-polymeri-
zation reduction.
[6] The copolymerization of propene with
allyl acetate is another way to reach PP that includes hydroxy
functionalities after hydrolysis, but the insertion rate of allyl
acetate was poor.
[7] Therefore, the coordination polymeri-
zation approach used to fabricate PP hasn/C29t been applied to
prepare P AA or hydroxy-containing PP , since even the Boc-
protected polar monomers are poisonous to the employed
coordination catalysts.
Allene compounds are widely employed as building
blocks in the field of organic synthesis due to their highly
active cumulative double bonds.
[8] They have also attracted
the attention of polymer scientists because the corresponding
polymers possess double bonds that can be transformed into
other functionalities, for example, through hydrogenation,
[9]
epoxidation,[10] and hydrosilylation,[11] in post-polymerization
modification steps. However, the high activity of the cumu-
lative double bonds causes difficulty in controlling the
polymer microstructures through either radical or cationic
polymerization.
[12] Well-controlled polymerization of allenes
is achieved by using coordination catalysts, of which the Ti-
based systems [10] , h3-allyl NiOCOCF 3,[13] and the rare-earth-
metal catalysts[14] display almost perfect 2,3-selectivity. Never-
theless, the resultant polymers contain internal C =C double
bonds that are chemically stable and resistant to further
transformation. On the other hand, 1,2-selective polymeri-
zation of allenes gives polymers with the active terminal C =C
double bonds, which is sterically disfavored.
Herein, we report the highly active and distinguished 1,2-
selective coordination polymerization of allene monomers

(Scheme 1) and its copolymerization with propylene by using
the rare-earth metal precursors (Scheme 2). The resultant
poly(allene)s have high molecular weights and are facilely
transformed into analogous P AAs through hydroboration/
oxidation reactions under mild conditions. Strikingly, the
copolymerization of propylene and allene monomers is also
successful to afford unprecedented hydroxy-functionalized
PP after post-polymerization modification. The mechanism
for the activity and 1,2-selectivity was elucidated through
DFT simulation, which indicated that the process is under
kinetic rather than thermodynamic control.
PNP-carbazolide scandium ( 1a ) and yttrium ( 1b ) bis-
(alkyl) complexes have been reported to show excellent
activity and perfect cis-1,4-selectivity in the activation of
[Ph
3C][B(C6F5)4] for the polymerization of conjugated diene
monomers.[15] Both were tested for catalyzing n-decylallene
polymerization (Table 1, entries 1 and 2) but were completely
inert. Then, constrained geometry configuration(CGC) cata-
lysts, namely fluorenyl rare-earth metal bis(alkyl) complexes
with methylene pyridine side arms [(Flu-CH
2-Py)Ln-
(CH2SiMe3)2(THF)n (Ln = Sc, n = 0, 2a ;Y , n = 1, 2b )] in
combination with [Ph 3C][B(C6F5)4] and Al iBu3 were
employed. The polymerization of n-decylallene with yttrium
precursor 2b afforded only trace amounts of polymer, in
contrast to its behavior in phenylallene polymerization, where
it was reported previously to exhibit high activity and pure
2,3-selectivity.
[14] Upon switching to the more Lewis acidic
scandium precursor 2a , the polymerization proceeded effi-
ciently and reached 90 % conversion in 24 h. The isolated
polymer showed 1,2-regularity (72 %; Table 1, entries 3 and
4). Therefore, we turned to the less bulky half-sandwich
thiophene-fused-cyclopentadienyl scandium complex 3,
which is highly active for ethylene polymerization.
[16] The
polymerization went smoothly to reach 92.2 % conversion
under the same conditions to with precursors 2 and gave
a poly( n-decylallene) with a moderate molecular weight
(M
n = 1.8 /C148 104 ; Table 1, entry 5). The 1H NMR spectrum of
the resultant polymer (Figure 1, top) shows two groups of
broad peaks at d = 5.21 and 2.8 ppm corresponding to the
terminal vinyl protons H
a and methine proton H b on the 1,2-
regulated polymer chains, while the broad resonances within
the range of d = 2.0 to 0.5 ppm are attributed to the alkyl
C
10H21 protons. The peak at d = 5.63 ppm corresponding to
the internal methylene protons Hc is rather weak. The ratio of
the integral intensities of H a :Hc indicates a 94 % 1,2-tacticity,
which is higher than that obtained from any other catalysts
reported to date.
Intrigued by these results, we investigated in detail the
catalytic performance of complex 3 under various conditions.
Representative data are shown in Table 2. Upon changing the
n-decylallene/Sc ratio from 100:1 to 500:1, the molecular
weight of the resultant poly( n-decylallene) increased corre-
spondingly from M
n = 1.8 /C148 104 to 3.6 /C148 104 while the molec-
ular-weight distribution was maintained (Table 1, entry 5;
Table 2, entries 1 and 2). This indicates that the polymeri-
zation is controllable and the active species is single-sited,
which avoids any side reactions and crosslinking products.
Notably, the addition of Al
iBu3 (Al:Sc = 10:1) to the above
binary system [Sc]/[Ph3C][B(C6F5)4] did not show any obvious

influence on the catalytic performances (Table 2, entry 3).
Upon lowering the polymerization temperature to 0 8C,
a higher-molecular-weight polymer with a distinguished 1,2-
regularity ( Mn = 3.7 /C148 104, 96 %) was afforded. Upon further
decreasing the temperature to /C020 8C and /C040 8C, the
polymerization still proceeded to give an over 85 % con-
version, albeit at a prolonged polymerization time. Mean-
while, the 1,2-selectivity increased strikingly to over 99 %
(Figure 1, middle). In the
13C NMR spectrum, the terminal
vinyl carbon C a shows a resonance at d = 109 ppm and the
ternary carbon C b displays a sharp singlet at d = 152 ppm,
whilst the methine carbon C c appears at d = 51 ppm. There
are no resonances from the other regularities, thus indicating
almost perfect 1,2-regularity (Figure 2), which is further
confirmed by the HSQC spectrum analysis (Figure S39).
Compared to the 2,3-selectivity observed for allene polymer-
ization, 1,2-selectivity means a spatially disfavored route,
therefore, the high recorded value of 1,2-selectivity is, as far as
we are aware, indeed unconventional. The physical properties
of poly(n-decylallene) products are strongly dependent on the
microstructure. The polymer with a 94 % 1,2-tacticity pos-
sesses a T
g value of /C027 8C without a melting point (Tm), while
that bearing an over 99 % 1,2-tacticity gives a melting point
Tm = 39 8C owing to its more regulated microstructure, albeit
containing long soft alkyl side chains (Figure 3).
The distinguished performances of complex 3 towards n-
decylallene drove us to explore the polymerizations of allene
derivatives bearing different substituents. Monomer B, which
contains an n-hexyl group (Scheme 1), was polymerized to
give poly( n-hexylallene) with the identical 1,2-regularity as
poly(n-decylallene), thus suggesting that the length of the side
alkyl chain has no obvious influence on the selectivity
(Table 2, entries 8 and 9). The polymerization of monomer
C, which possesses a terminal C =C double bond, exhibited
regioselectivity at the allene unit exclusively, thus indicating
the high reactivity of the cumulative double bonds compared
to discrete double bonds (Table 2, entries 10 and 11). T o
investigate the influence of polar substituents, monomers D,
E, F, and G were synthesized (Scheme 1). Monomer D has
a propyloxo fragment attached to the cumulative double
bonds. During the polymerization, the oxygen atom is geo-
metrically available to back-bite the active Sc
3+ ion together
with the cumulative unit, thereby generating a strong chelate
that retards the polymerization (Scheme S1 in the Supporting
Information). Replacing the n-C
6H13 species in D with
a phenyl group is anticipated to prevent oxygen from
poisoning the active species, and monomer F indeed could
be polymerized sluggishly to reach 42 % conversion in 72 h

albeit with a rather low 1,2-selectivity (13.0 %). This might be
attributed to weak back-biting chelation of the phenoxy
group to the active metal center to give a crowded and
variable coordination–insertion environment. Monomer E,
which bears the methylene unit between the cumulative
double bonds and phenoxy group, was completely inert since
it coordinates to the active species and then isomerizes to 1-
phenoxy-1,3-butadiene through 1,3-hydrogen shift.
[17] Strik-
ingly, monomer G, which contains a butyl spacer, polymerized
fluently to generate pure 1,2-tacticity (Table 2, entries 12–16).
The mechanism of this highly active and chemoselective
(1,2 vs. 2,3) performance for the polymerization of allenes A,
B, C,o r G was then elucidated by DFT calculations at the
(B3PW91) level based on catalysts 2a and 3. In the following,
only insertion of monomer B is considered as representative
of the allene polymerization. Experimentally, complex 2a
appears to be less 1,2-selective than catalyst 3. The two first
insertions (1,2 and 2,3) were computed for catalyst 2a (see
Figure S64). It was found that there is clear kinetic competi-
tion between the two insertions, which is in line with the
moderate selectivity of this complex for the 1,2-insertion.
Indeed, the first insertion seems to be 1,2 (barrier of 10.0 vs.
13.6 kcal mol
/C01), whereas the second one might be a 2,3
(11.9 kcal mol/C01 vs. 6.9 kcal mol /C01). On the other hand, the
reactivity of complex 3 seems very different (Scheme 3).
Interestingly, the 1,2-insertion appears to be kinetically
always more favorable than the 2,3 one (barrier of 7.0 vs.
10.4 kcal mol
/C01 for the first insertion and of 0.5 vs. 8.0 kcal
mol/C01 for the second one). This is in line with the greater
selectivity for the 1,2-insertion observed experimentally. This
selectivity appears to be due to the fact that no stable 1,2-
adduct can be formed whereas a stable 2,3 adduct can. The
stability of the latter therefore reduces the 2,3 reactivity.
However, it should be noted that 1,2-selectivity appears to be
kinetically driven since the 2,3-insertion product, which
appears to be a p-allyl, is thermodynamically favored. There-
fore, at high temperature, formation of the thermodynamic
product should be observed, thereby reducing the 1,2-
selectivity, whereas the 1,2-selectivity should be greater at
low temperature (low energy demand for the reaction). This is
in perfect agreement with the experimental results (Table 2,
entries 8 and 9). Therefore, the reaction sequence is con-
trolled by the kinetically facile 1,2-insertion but not by the
coordination of the monomer to the metal center. This finding
is quite unusual for classical coordination-insertion mecha-
nisms and is associated with steric repulsion between the
growing polymer chain and the allene, which prevents the
formation of a 1,2-adduct.
Hydrolysis of the obtained polymers was performed
through hydroboration with BH
3 followed by oxidation with
H2O2 under mild conditions. In the 1H NMR spectrum, the
peak at d = 5.21 ppm assigned to the terminal vinyl protons is
almost invisible, while the broad resonance at d = 3.75 ppm is
attributed to the methylene CH 2 group adjacent to the
hydroxy group, thus suggesting the rather high efficiency of
this post-polymerization modification (Figure 1, bottom). In
the FTIR (cm
/C01) trace, the characteristic C =C stretching
vibration at 1648 arising from 1,2-regulated poly(alkylallene)
is nearly absent while a strong and broad resonance at
3300 cm
/C01 is attributed to the stretching vibration of the newly
generated O/C0H bond (Figure S61).
The surface properties of the nonpolar poly(alkylallene) is
greatly improved after hydrolysis to decyl substituted P AA,
which gives a smaller static water contact angle (WCA) of
96.2
8 as compared to 107.7 8 for poly(alkylallene).[18]
Compared to the extensive investigations on functional-
izing polyethylene through coordination polymerization of
ethylene with polar monomers,
[3] that for polypropylene is
rather rare. One reason is that polypropylene cannot be
prepared through a radical mechanism, which avoids radical
copolymerization with vinyl acetylacetate; another is efficient
catalysts for propylene coordination polymerization are very
limited compared to those for
ethylene polymerization, thus
those that can survive in the
copolymerization with polar
monomers are scarce. The suc-
cess of highly 1,2-selective poly-
merization of the nonpolar
allene compounds prompted us
to attempt their copolymeriza-
tion with propylene using the
excellent precursor 3. Unfortu-
nately, only trace amounts of
polymer were obtained, which
might be due to intense compe-
tition between the two mono-
mers. Surprisingly, upon activa-

tion with [Ph3C][B(C6F5)4], complex 2a successfully mediated
the copolymerization of allene monomer A and propylene
with high activity comparable to that of propylene homopo-
lymerization and rather high 1,2-selectivity (80 %). Mean-
while the allene incorporation was sensitive to the propylene
fraction in the reaction vessel, which increased with a decrease
in propylene pressure and reaction temperature to reach up to
26.5 % (Table 3). This meant that after post-functionalization,
a polypropylene containing as high as a 26.5 % molar fraction
of hydroxy groups was realized for the first time.
In summary, we have demonstrated that the unconven-
tional highly 1,2-selective polymerization of polar and non-
polar alkylallene compounds can be achieved with high
activity by using rare-earth-metal catalytic systems. These
alkyl-substituted allene monomers are sterically demanding,
thus, from a catalytic precursor viewpoint, a more open
coordination sphere is a precondition to show activity for
allene polymerization. Half-sandwich thiophene-fused cyclo-
pentadienyl-ligated rare-earth metal precursors are sterically
less bulky than the pyridinyl methylene fluorenyl and the
tridentate PNP ligated rare-earth-metal precursors, and
exhibit higher activity. From the allene monomer viewpoint,
a long alkyl chain or a terminal double bond does not prohibit
polymerization but a polar oxygen atom can terminate the
polymerization by chelating to the active metal center. With
respect to chemoselectivity, the 1,2-selective polymerization
is under kinetic rather than thermodynamic control. This
work opens a new avenue to hydroxy modification of non-
polar polymers through copolymerization synthons while
avoiding the problem of catalysts being poisoned by the polar
groups. The copolymerizations of allenes with styrene and
conjugated dienes and other simple olefins is currently under
investigation.
